name: Maintainability
summary: How easily the system can be changed, tested, and operated over time — small edits stay safe, breakage is localized, and new engineers can reason about the flow.
description: Maintainability is the cost of the second, tenth, and hundredth change to a pipeline. It grows from modular transformations under version control, automated tests, declarative definitions, and a single source of truth for each concept, so a change in one place propagates predictably instead of rippling through bespoke jobs. Stacks built with software-engineering discipline let teams refactor with confidence; hand-rolled scripts and duplicated logic decay into fragile systems only their author understands.

mechanisms.name: Modular transformations
mechanisms.note: Composable, dependency-aware models with clear inputs and outputs let a change touch one node without rewriting the whole pipeline.

mechanisms.name: Version control and CI
mechanisms.note: Pipeline logic in Git with review and continuous integration makes every change auditable, revertible, and validated before it ships.

mechanisms.name: Automated data tests
mechanisms.note: Assertions on schema, uniqueness, and business rules catch regressions at build time so refactors are safe rather than a leap of faith.

mechanisms.name: Declarative pipeline definitions
mechanisms.note: Describing the desired state and dependencies rather than imperative steps lets the framework handle ordering, retries, and reruns consistently.

mechanisms.name: Single source of truth
mechanisms.note: Defining each metric or entity exactly once, with clear layer boundaries, removes the duplicated logic that makes changes risky and inconsistent.

manifestations.statement: A clean staging-to-marts split of small tested dbt models under version control means changes localize to one layer and CI catches regressions before they ship.
Warehouse-native SQL models with tests, lineage, and Git review bring software-engineering discipline to transformation, so the pipeline stays refactorable as it grows.
Explicit bronze/silver/gold boundaries with declarative, tested transformations make each promotion step independently changeable and easy to reason about.
Defining every metric exactly once removes duplicated logic across tools, so a business-rule change is a single edit instead of a hunt through dashboards.
One in-process engine and a handful of SQL or Python files mean the entire pipeline fits in one head, making changes trivially cheap to understand and test.
Rigid hub/link/satellite patterns make loads uniform and predictable, but the many-object model and downstream marts add moving parts every change must respect.
Well-understood dimensional patterns are maintainable, but conformed dimensions and SCD logic create cross-cutting dependencies that make some changes ripple widely.
Managed connectors keep replication low-touch, but schema drift at the source and merge logic downstream still demand ongoing attention to keep the mirror correct.
Warehouse-built profiles are refactorable, but identity-resolution rules and activation mappings accumulate special cases that make the logic progressively harder to change.
Declarative streaming SQL keeps definitions readable, but stateful operators, watermarks, and reprocessing make changes riskier to validate than batch models.
One streaming code path avoids duplication, but stateful processing, evolving schemas, and the difficulty of testing continuous logic raise the cost of each change.
Ingestion and chunking are modular, but retrieval tuning, prompt logic, and embedding-model changes lack strong test harnesses, so improvements are often trial-and-error.
Every business rule must be implemented and kept in sync across separate batch and speed codebases, deliberately doubling maintenance effort to serve both views.
Domain ownership keeps each product small, but many independently evolving teams and a shared platform contract trade local simplicity for real cross-domain coordination cost.
Bespoke hand-coded jobs with embedded, duplicated logic and little test coverage are brittle to change, and edits often break in places only the original author foresaw.
Schema-on-read pushes undocumented parsing logic into every consumer, so a source change forces uncoordinated edits across many independent readers.
Custom sync scripts straddling on-prem and cloud, often without tests or version control, become fragile glue that few engineers dare to modify.
Accumulated matching rules, survivorship exceptions, and stewardship overrides make the golden-record logic dense and risky to change without regressions.
A normalized enterprise core with many dependent marts creates deep dependency chains, so a model change can require coordinated updates across the whole EDW.
Keeping masking rules, tokenization vaults, classification tags, and access policies correct as schemas evolve is ongoing overhead that makes the zone harder to maintain than an open one.

tradeoffs.title: Latency
tradeoffs.note: Modular boundaries, abstraction layers, and declarative orchestration add indirection and serialization hops that a hand-fused pipeline would avoid.

tradeoffs.title: Cost efficiency
tradeoffs.note: Managed, well-integrated tools and mature frameworks that keep the system easy to change cost more than lean, hand-rolled components doing the minimum.

tradeoffs.title: Throughput
tradeoffs.note: Clean, generic, declarative transformations are rarely as raw-optimal as bespoke code tuned to the data, leaving some peak processing rate on the table.
